title: Treasury Seeks Public Comment on GENIUS Act Proposed Rulemaking (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Regarding the Issuance, Offering, and Sale of Payment Stablecoins in the U.S.)
date_evidence: Press Releases | Treasury Seeks Public Comment on GENIUS Act Proposed Rulemaking | August 17, 2026
key_claim: From 18 January 2027, the expected effective date of the GENIUS Act, digital asset service providers generally may not offer, sell or make available foreign-issued payment stablecoins unless the foreign issuer has the technological capability to comply with, and will comply with, any lawful order and any reciprocal arrangement between the US and the issuer's home jurisdiction; from 18 July 2028 they may not offer or sell any payment stablecoin to persons in the US unless it is issued by a licensed issuer. Comments are due within 60 days of Federal Register publication.
frame_summary: Treasury presents the Section 3 rule as delivering regulatory certainty and cementing the dollar's reserve-currency role, framing the foreign-issuer conditions as rules of the road rather than as market-access gatekeeping.
verbatim_quote: In addition, digital asset service providers generally may not offer, sell, or otherwise make available foreign-issued payment stablecoins unless the foreign issuer has the technological capability to comply with, and will comply with, the terms of any lawful order and any reciprocal arrangement between the United States and the issuer’s home jurisdiction.
verbatim_list: Beginning on January 18, 2027, the expected effective date of the GENIUS Act, a person generally may not “issue a payment stablecoin in the United States” unless the person has obtained an appropriate federal or state license.

Beginning on July 18, 2028, the Act further provides that digital asset service providers generally may not offer or sell any payment stablecoins to persons “in the United States” unless the payment stablecoins are issued by a licensed issuer.
Members of the public should submit comments in response to the NPRM within 60 days of publication in the Federal Register.
notes: Primary regulator press release accompanying the NPRM published in the Federal Register on 18 August 2026 (91 FR, doc 2026-16796). title: Targeted consultation on the review of Regulation on the Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA): consultation document
date_evidence: Consultation landing page (finance.ec.europa.eu, Targeted consultation on the review of MiCA Regulation): Opening date 20 May 2026 | Reference documents: 20 MAY 2026 Consultation document: Targeted consultation on the review of MiCA Regulation, English (635.98 KB - PDF)
key_claim: The Commission states that MiCA does not currently prohibit multi-issuer models and asks respondents whether MiCA should remain open to them (Question 30); it lists run risk and reserve depletion in the EU, unbalanced reserve distribution across jurisdictions, cross-border reserve transfer restrictions and regulatory arbitrage due to fungibility of tokens as the risks to rate (Question 29); and it asks whether an equivalence regime for global stablecoins should be introduced (Questions 40-41).
frame_summary: The Commission frames multi-issuance as a live policy choice to be settled on evidence about run and reserve-fragmentation risk, and treats third-country equivalence as the missing instrument in MiCA rather than as something to be ruled out.
verbatim_quote: Question 30. MiCA does not currently prohibit multi‑issuer models, nor does the EU have jurisdiction to determine how third country entities, that also have licensed entities in the EU, should be regulated in third country jurisdictions.
verbatim_list: Run risk and reserve depletion in the EU (e.g. cross‑border migration of tokens during stress leading to sudden increase of redemption pressure on EU issuers)
Regulatory arbitrage due to fungibility of tokens (e.g. operation across regimes exploiting differences in prudential or conduct rules)
You are invited to reply by 31 August 2026 at the latest to the online questionnaire
notes: Structural anchor (110 days old at scan date): the canonical EU primary for the multi-issuance question. The PDF carries no date on its title page; the date is read from the Commission's consultation landing page, which lists the document under Reference documents dated 20 MAY 2026 and records the deadline extension to 30 September 2026. Verbatim spans use the PDF's non-breaking hyphen in multi‑issuer / cross‑border. title: Deadline extended for consultation on the functioning of EU crypto-assets rules
date_evidence: Deadline extended for consultation on the functioning of EU crypto-assets rules | Date: 29/06/2026
key_claim: The Commission extended the MiCA review consultation by one month; both the public and the targeted consultation now remain open until 30 September 2026, with the targeted strand seeking feedback on current requirements and on segments not initially covered by MiCA.
frame_summary: The Commission presents the extension as giving stakeholders more time on a framework it is testing for fitness as markets and the wider regulatory landscape evolve, signalling that the review's scope is open rather than settled.
verbatim_quote: The consultation will now remain open until 30 September 2026, giving stakeholders additional time to contribute their views.
verbatim_list: We have extended the deadline for our consultation on EU crypto-asset rules by one month.

title: Treasury Proposes GENIUS Act Gatekeeping Rules with a Path for Foreign Issuers
date_evidence: Aug 25 2026 | On August 17, 2026, the Department of the Treasury (“Treasury”) issued a highly anticipated notice of proposed rulemaking
key_claim: The foreign-issuer restriction takes effect on 18 January 2027 before Treasury has established any process for determining whether a foreign issuer's home jurisdiction is comparable under Section 18(a); Treasury proposes that a digital asset service provider may rely on the foreign issuer's representation of lawful-order capability after reasonable due diligence; comments are due 19 October 2026; the one-year statutory deadline for GENIUS regulations lapsed in July with no bank-regulatory, BSA or AML rule finalised and the Federal Reserve's prudential rule not yet proposed.
frame_summary: Freshfields argues Treasury has read the statute permissively to open a direct US issuance path for foreign issuers, but that the sequencing leaves a gap in which exchanges carry the compliance risk on issuer representations, and expects that gap to dominate the comment period.
verbatim_quote: This sequencing produces a notable gap. The FPSI restriction becomes effective first even though Treasury has not yet established the process for determining whether an FPSI’s home jurisdiction maintains a comparable regulatory regime, such that the FPSI may operate in the United States under Section 18(a) of the GENIUS Act.
verbatim_list: It therefore proposes that a DASP may rely on an FPSI’s representation that the FPSI has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with lawful orders and reciprocal arrangements, provided that the DASP conducts reasonable due diligence.
As noted above, comments are due October 19, 2026, and we expect robust discussion of the issues highlighted above.

Although the one-year statutory deadline for issuing regulations lapsed in July, none of the bank regulatory, Bank Secrecy Act, or anti-money-laundering rules has been finalized, and a required rule establishing the Federal Reserve’s prudential framework has not yet been proposed.
notes: Major law-firm client analysis; Tier 2. Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at; sandbox has no network egress for the automated re-fetch.

title: Singapore Publishes Draft Legislation to Implement Its Stablecoin Framework
key_claim: On 1 September 2026 MAS published draft Payment Services Act amendments reversing its 2023 refusal of multi-jurisdictional issuance: a proposed section 100A would let MAS exempt, case by case, an arrangement from the Singapore-incorporation and full-local-reserve requirements, conditioned on the foreign co-issuer being supervised under a regime MAS deems substantively equivalent, aggregate reserves of at least 100% of global circulation with composition meeting the stricter regime, MAS-approved rebalancing or attribution models with daily records and monthly reporting, comparable redemption fees and timelines across jurisdictions, and group-wide recovery and wind-up planning; a separate recognition regime would admit a limited number of foreign-issued stablecoins; consultation closes 16 October 2026. The alert also records the Bank of England's draft Code of Practice with a temporary £40 billion issuance guardrail (22 June 2026) and the FCA's final issuer rules (30 June 2026).
frame_summary: Gibson Dunn reads the MAS package as convergent with the US, EU, UK and Hong Kong regimes on core protections and argues that the GENIUS Act is exporting US compliance requirements, so foreign frameworks built on substantive-equivalence tests are positioning themselves for a cross-border architecture led by US comparability.
verbatim_quote: The MAS has now reversed course, citing the considerable maturation of stablecoin regulation globally and the growing prevalence of MJI use cases.
verbatim_list: Exemptions will be conditioned on substantial safeguards, including: the foreign co-issuers being supervised under a regime the MAS deems substantively equivalent to the MAS-SCS framework (with weight given to bilateral supervisory cooperation arrangements); aggregate reserves across all issuing entities of at least 100% of global circulation at all times, with composition meeting the stricter of the applicable regimes; MAS-approved reserve rebalancing arrangements or stablecoin attribution models, supported by daily record-keeping and monthly reporting; comparable redemption fees and timelines across jurisdictions (to prevent redemption arbitrage and cross-border liquidity runs); and group-wide recovery and orderly wind-up planning.
The consultation closes on 16 October 2026, and the MAS will consult separately on the accompanying subsidiary legislation at a later date.
Foreign frameworks are therefore increasingly being designed with U.S. comparability in mind

the Bank of England is consulting on a draft Code of Practice for sterling-denominated systemic stablecoins (featuring a temporary £40 billion issuance guardrail per systemic stablecoin), which it intends to finalise by the end of 2026

The MAS has signalled that it expects to take a selective and risk-based approach to authorising stablecoin issuers and recognising foreign-issued stablecoins, anticipating that only a limited number of stablecoins will be authorised or recognised
notes: Used in place of the MAS media release and consultation paper (P015-2026, 1 September 2026), which the sandbox could not retrieve (the MAS page returned no body via web_fetch and the built-in browser lacks a site grant). Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.

title: Fit for Purpose? European Commission Launches Review of MiCA
date_evidence: June 10, 2026 | Skadden Publication / The Distributed Ledger
key_claim: The Commission has for the first time acknowledged that multi-issuance structures are not prohibited by MiCA; it is exploring safeguards including stronger redemption rights for tokens genuinely circulating in the EU, restricting direct redemption to clients of EU-authorised CASPs and differentiating retail and business redemption rights; MiCA has no mechanism for recognising third-country regimes; an equivalence regime could let multi-issuance structures rely on mutual recognition; about 227 CASPs are listed in the ESMA register across 25 EEA countries.
frame_summary: Skadden argues the review is a competitiveness-driven reassessment in which the equivalence regime is the most forward-looking proposal, and urges market participants to push for it so that globally circulating stablecoins can reach EU platforms.
verbatim_quote: Notably, the Commission has for the first time in the consultation acknowledged that multi-issuance structures are currently not prohibited by MiCA for all stablecoins.
verbatim_list: Currently, there is no mechanism under MiCA for recognizing or deferring to third-country regulatory frameworks.

Multi-issuance structures could rely on mutual recognition across jurisdictions, and stablecoins issued under comparable third-country frameworks could potentially become eligible for listing on EU exchanges.
Restricting direct redemption rights to clients of EU-authorized CASPs.
notes: Major law-firm analysis of the 20 May 2026 consultation; Tier 2. Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.

title: EU Parliament backs stablecoin multi-issuance, dismissing ban proposal
key_claim: The European Parliament adopted its digital-assets report by 390 votes to 86, asking that multi-issuance be put on a sound legal footing with safeguards, against the ESRB's recommendation that MiCA be read as not permitting it; Circle already issues USDC in the US and through its French entity with fully interchangeable tokens and reserves split by jurisdiction; national regulators have reached differing conclusions; the Commission consults until 30 September with a legislative proposal widely expected in 2027.
frame_summary: Ledger Insights argues the non-binding vote matters because own-initiative reports set Parliament's negotiating line for the 2027 legislation, placing Parliament squarely against the ESRB on whether fungible cross-border coins should be allowed.
verbatim_quote: This week the European Parliament adopted a report on digital assets by a large majority, with 390 votes in favor and 86 against.
verbatim_list: Circle issues USDC in the United States and separately through its French entity under Europe’s MiCA regulation, with the tokens fully interchangeable and the reserves split between issuance jurisdictions.
The Commission is consulting on a review of MiCA until September 30, and a legislative proposal is widely expected in 2027.
In the meantime national regulators have reached their own conclusions about whether the structure is allowed, creating precisely the sort of legal patchwork that MiCA was designed to prevent.
notes: Specialist trade press; the article's opening section is free and the remainder is behind a Pro paywall. Vote tally cross-checked against the roll-call record (HowTheyVote.eu: 390 for, 86 against, 134 abstentions, 7 July 2026, A10-0186/2026, resolution P10_TA(2026)0251). Quote confirmed by hand via web_fetch at verified_at.

title: Stablecoins, euro numérique : le gouverneur de la Banque de France fixe le cap (Governor Moulin's VivaTech speech, 19 June 2026)
key_claim: Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin told VivaTech on 19 June 2026 that stablecoin capitalisation had grown from under $5 billion in 2019 to $300 billion in 2026, with dollar-backed coins at 99% of it, and called for MiCA to be strengthened, including tighter rules on non-euro stablecoins in everyday payments and on multi-issuer models where the same stablecoin is issued both inside and outside the EU.
frame_summary: Cryptoast reads the speech as confirming the Banque de France and ECB line of openness to tokenisation but firmness against dollar stablecoins, and asks why no euro stablecoin has reached dollar scale, pointing to MiCA's deposit floors and interest ban.
verbatim_quote: Emmanuel Moulin appelle à mieux réguler les stablecoins non libellés en euros utilisés pour les paiements du quotidien, ainsi que les modèles multi-émetteurs où un même stablecoin est émis à la fois dans et hors de l’UE.
verbatim_list: Le nouveau gouverneur de la Banque de France a rappelé que leur capitalisation cumulée, inférieure à 5 milliards de dollars en 2019, atteint désormais 300 milliards de dollars en 2026.
Le problème est que les stablecoins adossés au dollar représentent 99 % de cette capitalisation.
notes: French-language specialist press report of the governor's speech (multi-language pass). The speech itself is on banque-france.fr (De l'innovation à la souveraineté monétaire : trouver le bon équilibre) and, in English, on bis.org (central bankers' speeches, 22 June 2026); neither full text could be parsed in the sandbox (the banque-france.fr URL was outside the fetch provenance set and the BIS PDF returned unreadable text), so the Tier 3 report is used and treated directionally.
